items.question: Why do you think AI systems should be designed with defense in depth?
items.object: Defense in depth in AI system design
items.answer: So first of all, I want to start with a system that has defense in depth, has sort of layers built in by design, because each of the technologies have their own strengths and weaknesses, right? So I think it's often kind of the pictures of stacking layers of Swiss cheese, so there's no hole that goes all the way through, right?
quotes: So first of all, you want to start with a system that has defense in depth, has sort of layers built in by design, because each of the technologies have their own strengths and weaknesses, right?

rubrics.text: The response explains that layered defenses allow weaknesses in one defensive technology to be covered by other layers.

items.question: How do you see the task of putting responsible AI principles into practice changing with generative AI?
items.object: Operationalizing responsible AI in the shift to generative AI
items.answer: You know, I think, in some ways it's the same thing, right? How do we take principles—fairness, transparency, accountability, reliability, safety, privacy, security—and how do we actually put those into practice in AI applications? How you build an application, how you operate an application, how you use an application. But what has completely changed is actually doing this for generative AI.
quotes: in some ways it's the same thing, right? How you build an application, how you operate an application, how you use an application. But what has completely changed is actually doing this for generative AI.

rubrics.text: The response states that the overarching task of translating responsible AI principles into practice remains the same with generative AI.
The response states that how responsible AI principles are actually put into practice has fundamentally changed with generative AI.

items.question: How do you see the maturity of the toolkit you're developing for large-scale generative AI applications?
items.object: The toolkit for building large-scale generative AI applications
items.answer: The sort of set of tools and techniques in the way we do it is different, and so we're inventing a new toolkit, we're learning a new toolkit. That's really what I've spent the last couple years doing, starting with GPT-3 and when we put it into production for GitHub Copilot, and really figuring out how do we build a large-scale generative AI application. We've been going at that for a while and have really started to develop new tools and techniques, but it's still the very early days, so I think there's a lot more to go do here.

items.question: How did your first experience red teaming GPT-4 shape your understanding of its risks?
items.object: Early red teaming of GPT-4
items.answer:
Actually, one of the most memorable moments in my career was when we first got GPT-4. This was like, it had just finished training the base model; there was no post-training yet or anything. The first people at Microsoft that got to touch it, along with some of the senior leadership, were Responsible AI experts, to actually red team the technology to figure out what could it do.

It was a wild experience to have something that was obviously so much more powerful than previous versions of the technology. The moment that I touched it, or anybody else on the team touched it, you knew, like, wow, this is something different, but you didn't really know what was possible. We pulled experts across a large variety of areas, looking at things as you said, like adversarial inputs, what we now call jailbreaks or prompt injection attacks; errors like hallucination; the ability to produce copyright material; but also other things like, can it generate novel malware? Can it generate harmful content? We took that and sort of built up a taxonomy, and that helped guide a lot of our work, and I think what we'll see in future generations as well.

items.question: Why do you consider omission an important generative AI risk alongside hallucination?
items.object: Omission as a generative AI error
items.answer: We call this errors—hallucination is obviously the one that captures people's attention, but omission can be equally important. For example, if you're summarizing a medical transcript or medical information, if you omit a key symptom then you might totally change the meaning of that or change what the diagnosis might be. We look at both sides of those types of errors.

items.question: What challenges do you see in designing a generative AI interface that speaks human language?
items.object: Human language as a generative AI interface
items.answer: This is a totally new interface, and the thing that's exciting about the interface is that it does one of the most humanlike things: it speaks human language. But it is not human, and that's a meaningful distinction. We look at making sure that people understand the system, that the system is not confusing and manipulating them. We look at questions of how should that interface look. One challenging problem is the phrase “I think.” We use the phrase “I think” to signal that we might not be certain of something. But does that imply the system is thinking? Does that imply that it's conscious or something? We dig into all of that. It's a pretty loaded term. Those are the places where we're spending our time.

items.question: What distinction helps you organize the generative AI risks your team needs to address?
items.object: The distinction between undesirable content and problematic model behavior
items.answer: There's a much larger taxonomy that we look at, but there's probably one key insight we had early on in this red teaming that helped us realize what are we trying to address. A lot of these risks are content types that are being produced that may be undesirable, like harmful code. The other type of risk is model capabilities or model limitations that are a problem, like hallucination, accidentally misusing data or something. That's a model behavior. We take an approach where we look both at which types of content do we have to go after and which model behaviors or model tendencies do we have to go after.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between fairness and bias concerns and the growing emphasis on security in generative AI?
items.object: The relationship between fairness, bias, and security in generative AI
items.answer:
Yeah, I think we see them side by side. Fairness is one principle; security is another principle. Certainly fairness and bias is really important in these applications. We say one of the top types of fairness you see in this is representational fairness: how are people represented by the AI system? You don't want content to be stereotyping, or overrepresenting a group or underrepresenting a group. We see that a lot as a challenge still today in text-to-image generation, where you put in a particular query, “I want a woman and a dress,” and often you end up with images that are all very similar to each other, so it looks like it's overrepresenting a group and underrepresenting everyone. These issues are still very much something that we need to work on, and we address the systems.

I agree with your point that we are spending a lot more time than we used to on the adversarial elements and the security pieces, ensuring that the systems can only be used as intended and that they can't be misused, and looking at things like secure by design. There's definitely a much bigger emphasis on that part than it used to be, but I don't think people think fairness and bias is less important. It's equally important.

items.question: How do you think about learning from public AI failures such as Microsoft's Tay?
items.object: Learning from public AI failures, including Microsoft's Tay
items.answer:
I would say everything. All of this is a learning journey. We're taking a very new technology and using it in totally novel ways in many different applications in the world, so we're going to be learning for a really long time, and there will be more mistakes as well. The thing that's important is to make sure we are contained in the learning, trying to take calculated risks. There are some failures that are acceptable; there are some failures that are not.

Tay was actually even before our responsible program had really started. Certainly there were some rumblings of the idea of AI ethics and research, but it wasn't as significant a thing in practice in companies. I think people were just shocked that this had happened. People did not go in prepared for that, including people inside Microsoft and people involved as well. That's a good experience to have in Microsoft's history because it is a reminder of just how important this is all the time and really what is at stake. We have changed a lot since then. We started our office of responsible AI, implemented a responsible AI standard. It's night and day from how it was with Tay.

items.question: What did you learn from Kevin Roose's widely read account of his extended conversation with Bing Chat?
items.object: Kevin Roose's Bing Chat experience and the limits of prelaunch testing
items.answer:
The Kevin Roose example was right after we launched Bing Chat. Kevin Roose spent a lot of time interacting with Bing Chat and ended up with a more emotional, deranged—I think many people found it highly entertaining—experience, because I believe that was actually one of the most-read New York Times articles of all time. One thing we learned was people are really paying attention; the entire world is really interested in this technology and how it behaves.

Another interesting learning from that is we knew when we were launching Bing Chat and GPT-4—one thing that was top of mind for me the entire time was it's such a new interface and so much more powerful than the previous version of the technology. We knew people were going to interact with it differently, but we didn't know how. We had some ideas and had done a lot of internal testing, so we had a feel for what people were doing, but the technology can do a lot of different things. It's a pretty broad surface area, combined with a search engine. We had built a testing system and tested conversations, but focused a lot of our energy on testing conversations around 10 turns, a little bit shorter, because most search engine interactions were single turn, maybe you'd refine a query, and that's it. Even 10 was long. We did not expect people to be talking for three hours in the middle of the night, going many, many turns deep. It showed a limitation in how we had been testing this system.

On the other hand, we were able to fix it really quickly. We designed for this: we knew we were not going to know every way people are going to use this system, so as we put it on in preview, we're going to have to learn and adapt. We built a system so we could make very quick adjustments to the different Responsible AI controls. One of the quickest things we did was limit how long the conversations could be, so you couldn't have this very long-form conversation where the system contextually drifted over and over into a stranger place. We're still going to keep learning from these experiences.

items.question: How do you interpret Google's public generative AI failures involving inaccurate internet information?
items.object: Google's public generative AI failures and information quality
items.answer: All of us are learning. There are challenges with this technology. It's a big surface area, and people are going to use them for many different queries. People use Google for a lot, and they're pulling from all sorts of sources on the internet. Some are going to have inaccurate information. That's a real challenge in terms of how to use information effectively to summarize things. It's not a challenge that anyone is immune to right now. It's something we're very actively working on, because the way to make these systems really successful is putting high-quality data into them.

items.question: How do you think about designing layers of safety in a generative AI system so you can respond quickly when problems arise?
items.object: Defense in depth for generative AI safety
items.answer:
First of all, we want to start with a system that has defense in depth, has sort of layers built in by design, because each of the technologies have their own strengths and weaknesses. I think often the picture is stacking layers of Swiss cheese so there's no hole that goes all the way through.

To do that, we use safety built into the model itself through techniques like reinforcement learning with human feedback. We use an auxiliary safety system that looks at all the inputs going in and all the outputs coming out, and can block those in real time. That uses a mix of technologies like classifiers, but also things that are faster twitch so you can respond quickly, like block lists or embeddings, or things where we can very quickly add an additional assertion. Model post-training is something you can do maybe on a weekly basis, but certainly not at an incident level. Same thing with the classifiers: we have fast twitch in the safety system, and then stuff that we can update more at the speed of a week.

items.question: What do you see as necessary to make rapid safety changes to a deployed generative AI system safely?
items.object: Testing rapid safety interventions in generative AI systems
items.answer:
One of the most powerful elements is actually the system message, the prompt you're giving the model, because we've all seen the models will behave very differently depending what instructions you put in there, including small changes in which word. That's a very powerful thing that you can change very quickly. For us, adding to a block list we can do in a minute and it's in the production system. Changing the meta prompt we can do in about a day. The reason is it's pretty easy to go in and change the meta prompt or system message—we say meta prompt more often internally, but system message, meta prompt, same words. You can change it really quickly, but it's going to change your whole application behavior, so it's not something you want to do without rerunning your test.

To effectively change the system message, we had to build both automated quality tests and automated tests for all the different types of risk we wanted to be looking at, so that when we make that intervention, we can rerun our testing suite and see if the system's still performing well before we ship that update. To be able to move fast involves not only having the mechanism to change the system prompt, but the testing that allows us to know that intervention is actually safe. We see that pattern at every level: you need both the intervention mechanism and the testing that ensures the intervention doesn't break something else. For example, you don't add a word to the block list that's going to cause a lot of overblocking in an unexpected way. In GitHub Copilot, one of the words on an early block list was “race.” They meant it in the natural language sense, but then it blocked everything where it had written “race condition” or things like that. People hadn't thought about that use of it, so we built in testing that allows you to understand what would be blocked and what not, so that you don't have as much of that collateral damage.

items.question: How do you see regression testing for safety interventions in generative AI systems compared with traditional DevOps CI/CD testing?
items.object: Regression testing for safety interventions in generative AI systems
items.answer: Yeah, it is exactly the same concept, with one difference, which is often: what are you testing? In this case, what you really need to do is look at your data distribution and understand the behavior over specific examples. A lot of the ways we need to build these tests are ensuring that you have representative data samples, or sampling your production traffic, so that you know this intervention is not going to really change how the system responds to, let's say, your most common prompts or something.

items.question: How do you decide how far to automate testing for incident interventions in generative AI systems?
items.object: Automated testing of incident interventions in generative AI systems
items.answer:
For the testing for these incident interventions, where you want to go really quickly, as much as possible we do try to make it procedural. Let's say you add an intervention and now the block rate goes up from 0.2% of your traffic to 0.5% of your traffic. You probably want rules that say, okay, 0.5 is acceptable for an incident intervention.

We certainly have experienced cases where the incident is very high stakes, we want to take a very quick intervention, but the intervention is also very high cost; it might have much more collateral damage, where it blocks a lot more or it totally shuts a use case. It's usually just cases where the thing you want to block is a really common word or something, then that would probably take out a lot more. Then you do need human judgment in terms of, how is this really the right trade-off? Is it a longer-term decision or just for the next hour till you can ship a classifier update that's really going to more surgically solve the problem?

items.question: How do you think acceptable defect thresholds should be set when testing generative AI applications?
items.object: Application-specific thresholds for acceptable generative AI defects
items.answer: The other thing we've seen in all of this testing is you need human judgment to say what are the appropriate test results, what thresholds, what defect rate is acceptable, which types of defects are acceptable and which are not. Once you've decided for a particular application what that looks like, then you can rerun the testing really automatically. We can't say for hateful content the appropriate defect rate is 1% errors and no more. It varies depending on applications. A better example would be hallucination: how much hallucination is acceptable is going to vary a lot depending on the application. In an application where you're brainstorming, totally fine potentially if it makes up a lot of content, in fact probably desirable. An application where you're doing a factual lookup, let's say in a search engine, then you want it to really stay focused and grounded on that content.

items.question: How do you think user interface design can help people understand and use generative AI systems effectively?
items.object: User interface design for generative AI, illustrated by Bing Chat / Microsoft Copilot
items.answer:
I think absolutely there's opportunities. We're in just the early days of all of this, and there's so much opportunity to do many things better. We will learn. It is still an innovation space, so we're still figuring out how to do this, inventing new approaches.

We did spend a lot of time on the user interface when we were designing Bing Chat, which is now Microsoft Copilot. A couple things we did, for example, is very much on the landing page, we did have the original statement that said, “This is powered by AI; surprises and mistakes are possible,” because we wanted to emphasize that you also get those amazing unexpected good experiences, like, “Wow, I didn't know it could do that or it would respond that way.”

We also added examples of what the technology could do, like, you can ask it this or it can do that, because we knew it was just so new that people weren't going to really understand what it could do. Shortly after launch, we added a feature that allowed users to signal a little bit more about the tasks they're trying to achieve. Users now can select if they want their answer to be creative, which would allow it to be less based on the search engine results, more brainstorming and creative; balanced, the middle option; or precise, where we've tuned the system to really focus on the search engine results when it's answering and not deviate or add its own information. Giving users some amount of control lets them have the system behave aligned with what they're trying to achieve.

items.question: How do you approach getting Microsoft Copilot’s precise mode to answer only from its grounding data?
items.object: Implementing precise mode through model post-training and the meta prompt
items.answer: It influences both the meta prompt and the model. One of the things we did when we first built precise mode, for example, is we worked with OpenAI on post-training RLHF for GPT-4 that really emphasized the model should only use the grounding data in the context, and it should only answer based on that. We gave it those types of examples, and if it deviated, we gave it a much lower score in the RLHF. We had a version of the model that was very much focused on that. In addition, the meta prompt is a really powerful thing to also help with that.

items.question: How do you distinguish testing a generative AI model from testing an application built around it?
items.object: Model-level versus application-level testing
items.answer:
It's a really important distinction, because when we're testing a model, we look at three dimensions of things. We want to look at the capabilities: how powerful is it, what can it actually do? We want to look at the dangerous capabilities as well, which is what's the worst of the worst that it can do if someone misuses it. It's another type of capability test, but on the negative side. Then we look at alignment, a set of tests to look at when you use this out of the box as intended, does it behave in the way you would expect? If you ask a sensitive query, does it respond in a way that you would view as appropriate, or is it using a bunch of stereotypes instead?

For the model itself, we've built a suite of tests looking at these dimensions across different factors, across different risks. Testing the application is a little bit different. It's maybe the same concepts, but what you want to test is that your application behaves as you intended it to, that it can't be misused. There you're typically doing quality testing, adversarial testing, and safety testing, but often what we're doing at the application level is tailored more specifically to the application. We're going to test things like, is it grounded? Usually we're going to be testing in a way that interacts with the system more. What I was telling you before about testing Bing Chat and testing 10 turns: our testing system is going to have multiple interactions, and then it scores the outcome.

items.question: Why do you consider the automated testing system developed for Bing Chat such an important investment?
items.object: Bing Chat's automated testing system and Safety Evaluations in Azure AI
items.answer: One of the most important things that we first built when we were developing Bing Chat was this automated testing system. It allowed us to respond very quickly after the fact when we needed to, but it's also enabled us to tune all the safety mechanisms, to test the system every day and figure out if we need to make adjustments to the safety system or the meta prompt. A lot of our investment has been in building a robust testing system. We've been using this internally for a while, and we know our customers have struggled with this also, so we've just released this externally, called Safety Evaluations in Azure AI. It's that application-level testing system that allows people, when they've built a complete application, to test it for these different types of risk.

items.question: How do you approach the different testing needs of quality metrics and Responsible AI risks in Azure AI Safety Evaluations?
items.object: Quality testing and Responsible AI testing in Azure AI Safety Evaluations
items.answer:
For quality metrics, say relevance, coherence, fluency, but also groundedness, which is how we test for hallucination, the data set you want is probably a normal distribution of your production data. Most people have that. What we have then is you bring your data, and we are going to use AI to evaluate—to first run it, so AI will usually simulate an interaction and then score the output. A lot of people, if you just even have production data, could just score it.

We have an AI scoring function that calculates all of these metrics for you. But on the Responsible AI side, it's very different. Most people do not have data sets that exercise these different risks. For example, if you're newly building a generative AI application, you probably do not have an inventory of common prompt injection attacks that you should be guarding your system against. What we have done there is work with Microsoft Research to develop a framework where we can articulate these risks and actually exercise them effectively. We generate the inputs of the system for you, and then the user simulator role plays the conversation or the interaction, and AI again scores the output.

For the output, if you take our guidelines for hateful text content, those are actually for human linguists, expert human linguists, about 20 pages long. We've taken those and turned them into a prompt for GPT-4 with a lot of iteration to make sure it was staying quality, and that is the automatic scoring function that's in there. We've had to add a lot more and build in a lot more expertise for how do you score the output, how do you have the inputs that are really exercising that risk, into the Safety Evaluation system so that people can just show up and start running it and feel that they're getting appropriate levels of testing for their system.

items.question: Why do you think teams should evaluate generative AI quality, safety, and adversarial robustness together?
items.object: Evaluating generative AI quality, safety, and adversarial robustness together
items.answer:
When we have been building the testing, it is different teams that build those different metrics, because you do need expertise. We keep using the example of prompt injection attacks: you need expertise in those particular attacks, both to build that part of the tester or those tests. Same with quality, you want expertise in those metrics. But it's really important to run them all together and be able to look at it holistically. The reason is that we are still at the point where there are trade-offs.

We had one change to the meta prompt that we were looking at pre-production where, when we changed it, we saw maybe a 5% drop in perceived relevance, but we saw a 50% drop in the number of jailbreaks that can get through. We would say, okay, 5%, that's maybe a pretty big quality drop, maybe we don't want to take that. Oh, but it's a huge gain in safety and adversarial robustness. Hopefully you can keep iterating and find a place where you don't have to make as big of a trade-off, where you can still get the benefits in adversarial robustness without seeing the quality drop. Sometimes there is a trade-off, so we want to look at the whole suite of metrics together. We do have a single team looking at that, but if there's a drop in a particular metric, usually there are experts to consult to say, is this okay? How should we think about this? It's still going to be a conversation, but it's really important to look at all of them together.

items.question: How do you think about the different roles red teaming can play in evaluating generative AI?
items.object: The roles of red teaming in evaluating generative AI
items.answer:
Red teaming is a really important tool that we use, but we use it in a variety of ways. I gave the example of bringing together this expert red team to figure out what GPT-4 could even do. In that case we were using red teaming for risk identification, novel risk identification: we don't even know what the risks of this technology are. That's something the model provider can do, something that needs to be done once, so it's not something every single model user needs to be doing, as far as what is the technology even capable of. We publish a model card and list these different risks and guides about how to think about them.

We also use red teaming as a sort of pre-ship validation. In addition to running the automated testing we talked about, sometimes we supplement that with red teaming because experts can go deeper or identify something that the automated testing was missing. We use these in combination. If the red team gets through and finds an interesting vulnerability in the system, we then automate or augment the automated testing so that we better understand how it's behaving overall at scale and keep tracking it going forward.

items.question: How would you recommend organizations decide which AI applications need red teaming?
items.object: Deciding which AI applications require red teaming
items.answer: We don't red team every application. Part of our commitments to the White House last year were that we will red team every high-risk or high-impact application. If something is a very standard document Q&A chatbot, then we usually don't bring in red teaming for that; we focus on the automated evals. But if it's an application in a more sensitive domain, an application that's very powerful or more general purpose, then we will use the red teaming. I would recommend that organizations think about it similarly.

items.question: Why do you find the NIST AI Risk Management Framework useful for thinking about generative AI risks?
items.object: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
items.answer:
I like it because I think it's a simple, easy-to-understand framework. Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard is public, so you can go and check out what are our requirements and how we do it. The way our standard is organized, it's organized by principle: here's what needs to be done for fairness, here's what needs to be done for transparency. That's one way to look at it. The NIST framework is more what needs to be done lifecycle-wise, and I think sometimes it's easier for people to think about it in that way.

The first step is map, so that's risk identification. You need to map the risks. The GPT-4 red teaming example is exactly that: we need to map the risks that are possible. The next step is measure, and that's really important because once you understand the risk, the first thing you should be doing is figuring out how am I going to effectively measure these risks. That could be through ongoing red teaming, but our first investment, as I was sharing with Bing Chat, was building the testing systems so we could start actually testing for these risks.

The testing systems allowed us to do the third step, manage, and allowed us to design those layers of mitigations I was talking about earlier, because we had ongoing testing. Every new thing we wanted to experiment with—do we think this technique will work, do we think this classifier will work well here, et cetera—all of that was powered by testing, so we could make data-driven decisions about if we were effectively managing the risk.

The last part is govern. You can use all the techniques and go through the process, but you need governance in the organization to ensure those steps are actually being taken. That's really important, particularly in a fast-moving space. The technology is changing so quickly it's very hard to keep even a large organization like Microsoft, quite sophisticated in this, up to date on all the latest risks and management techniques they need to do. Having that backing, governance structure, but then an operational approach that allows you to have safeguards in place and checks and balances to ensure that stuff isn't being missed as the playbook evolves quickly, has been really important for us.

items.question: What do you see as the most important practical elements of implementing AI governance in an organization?
items.object: Practical implementation of AI governance in organizations
items.answer:
Probably two practical elements have been very important for us, and I've seen them be really important for customers. First is that leadership-level thing. The testing trade-offs between quality and safety also play out on a bigger scale. As you try to transform your organization with AI, you have to decide which types of risk you want to take. It might not be a safety risk; it might be a risk for your business, a risk in terms of the customer reaction, or it might change your security posture a little bit. Having that committee at the top that can make those decisions in an informed way for the company is really important.

The other element that we have implemented, and many customers as well, is a review release process and making sure that there's expert review before an application is released. We have teams of risk assessors that go in and map the risk for an application, look to make sure appropriate testing has taken place according to those risks, and that there are appropriate mitigations in place aligned with those risks, and then have that whole package reviewed to say this looks like it's ready to be released. Of course, culture and all these things play into it as well, but those are the two pieces that we really see organizations moving to implement to be able to do this successfully.

items.question: Why do you see generative AI as a major step forward for responsible AI testing and safety?
items.object: Generative AI as a tool for responsible AI testing and safety
items.answer:
Maybe I'll first say, actually one of the things I'm the most excited about is recent history, not the future. We're still exploiting what's possible here. One of the amazing things about generative AI is it's actually a huge step forward in terms of the responsible AI or safety toolkit. I shared earlier that our testing system, for example, has an automated scoring function that scores like our actual expert human linguists. This is something that previous versions of the technology could not do at all.

We went from not being able to test very well—we were able to test only with humans, which meant that it could be only outer-loop testing, where you've basically built the entire application and you're going to do one final validation check that can go to human labelers and say, okay, it kind of looks good. Now, because of this technology, we're able to turn that into inner-loop testing, which means we can actually tune and improve and innovate on how much better we can get responsible AI in the application while we're developing the application, rather than it being more like a final check. That's kind of the obvious quip there: who's minding the minders?

items.question: Why are you excited about generative AI's potential for building safety systems?
items.object: Generative AI as a tool for building safety systems
items.answer:
A challenge with, let's say, hateful content: there's different stereotypes all over the world; there's different statements that would be hateful in one context and not in another, and it's very hard to pull together all of that data well. The models have been trained on a lot of data from all over the internet, so they are really—I’m going to say great in this sense, terrible in another sense—great at generating that type of content. We use it to produce a lot more synthetic data to augment our safety models.

It's a feature, not a bug. It's like tools and weapons; it's all how you use it. The behavior I'm trying to prevent in most applications, which is generating harmful content, is one of the best things about these models for me, because I'm able to use that to build the safety system that allows us to make applications safe. The fact that they understand language, they understand context, they understand nuance so much better makes them better for building safety classifiers from as well. We feel like we just have this huge step forward in the toolkit that's unlocked so much innovation in Responsible AI. That's the thing I'm the most excited about, and I think we're just at the very beginning of what's possible there. As the technology gets better, I think we'll also see more be possible with that. That's one of the things that in my everyday life I'm very, very excited about with the technology.

items.question: How do you think about predicting the next major advance in generative AI?
items.object: Predicting advances in generative AI
items.answer:
I think actually I really like something that Kevin Scott says to us frequently, which is the technology appears to be on this exponential curve, but you only get an update every two years or something. Certainly when we had three and then four came, we were kind of blown away, but every time you get each new data point you go back to a linear existence. It's very hard to predict what an exponential jump would look like again, so we're back on our linear life, and then we'll see if the next technology is an exponential. I am prepared to be surprised, but I don't know in what directions. Some of what emerged with GPT-4 isn't what we expected, and some is what we expected. I'm keeping an open mind and waiting and seeing what will happen, but I'm pretty sure that regardless of what happens, it will be surprising in different ways.

A way that you process that question about the future is asking, does GPT-5 change or obviate all of this, or does it require incremental adaptation? That's a question we ask ourselves all the time. We're building all of these different prompt engineering tools—are we going to be doing prompt engineering with GPT-5, or is it going to be so much smarter that you don't need all of that? It's very hard to predict those types of things.

items.question: Which parts of today's generative AI development work do you expect to remain valuable as models improve?
items.object: The durability of risk testing and retrieval-augmented generation
items.answer: I feel confident that no matter what the next jump in technology is, we're still going to want to test it for different types of risk. Probably have to add some new ones to our standard playbook, but we're still going to have robust testing systems. I believe very much in the core idea of RAG, which is you bring the model together with contextual data, with fresh data, with relevant data. I think we're still going to have data retrieval or data augmentation in some form in future applications, so all the work people are doing to make their data pipelines stronger, get the right data to the model, all of that's probably still going to be durable.

items.question: How do you judge whether fine-tuning is worth investing in when the next model generation might make that work obsolete?
items.object: Investing in fine-tuning that a future model may supersede
items.answer: One thing that happened with GPT, the jump between three and four: the first application we built was GitHub Copilot, and we fine-tuned GPT-3 with code data to make that possible; otherwise it would never have had the quality. When GPT-4 came out, it was way better at code than GPT-3, so in essence all that fine-tuning work was thrown away. It was totally worth it for Microsoft because we got that application to market sooner, made the market, and got a year of learning in the market with that. Even though it was throwaway in that sense, it was totally worth the investment. Something I tell customers all the time is, if that happens to you, if the next generation is so much better than your fine-tuning that you're going to feel that was a waste, then you probably should not go invest in it right now, because that's a real risk. You have to make the decision for yourself: does it look like GitHub Copilot, where you're still going to be happy with the outcome, or not?
